### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).
We then subjected tfLiveDrop mice to a high‑fat diet/streptozotocin‑induced type 2 diabetes (T2D) model ( Figure

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).
We then subjected tfLiveDrop mice to a high‑fat diet/streptozotocin‑induced type 2 diabetes (T2D) model ( Figure

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).
We then subjected tfLiveDrop mice to a high‑fat diet/streptozotocin‑induced type 2 diabetes (T2D) model ( Figure

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).
We then subjected tfLiveDrop mice to a high‑fat diet/streptozotocin‑induced type 2 diabetes (T2D) model ( Figure

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).
We then subjected tfLiveDrop mice to a high‑fat diet/streptozotocin‑induced type 2 diabetes (T2D) model ( Figure

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).

### ABSTRACT
Lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets (LDs), is central to cellular lipid homeostasis, yet its dynamic regulation in living organisms has remained largely unobservable in real time. To overcome this barrier, we recently developed the mCherry‑eGFP‑LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mice, in which a pH‑sensitive tandem fluorescent probe targeted to LDs via the GPAT4‑derived LiveDrop domain enables real‑time, single‑cell visualization of lipophagic flux in vivo. Using tfLiveDrop mice, we uncovered pronounced organ heterogeneity in basal lipophagy, identified an organ‑specific lipophagic inhibition in type 2 diabetes, and revealed a previously unrecognized developmentally programmed lipophagy induction that drives renal metabolic maturation. Together, these findings demonstrate that tfLiveDrop is a sensitive and versatile reporter for in vivo lipophagy research.
KEYWORDS: Lipophagy, lipid droplets, fatty acid oxidation, metabolic reprogramming, type 2 diabetes, kidney development
Lipophagy involves the sequestration of lipid droplets (LDs) into autophagosomes and their subsequent delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Its dysfunction has been linked to steatosis, diabetic complications, atherosclerosis, and neurodegeneration. Despite its importance, studying lipophagy in living organisms has been remarkably challenging. Conventional approaches, like electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and bulk LD staining, provide only static snapshots and cannot visualize the dynamic process of lipophagic flux. A genetically encoded, sensitive reporter capable of dynamically visualize lipophagic flux at cellular resolution in vivo was urgently needed.
To address this gap, we generated the tandem fluorescent LiveDrop (tfLiveDrop) reporter mouse [ 1 ]. Similarly to the pioneering system developed to measure mitophagy in vivo, in mice, the design leveraged two key principles. First, we fused a pH‑sensitive mCherry‑eGFP tandem fluorophore to the LiveDrop domain

### Figure 1.
Schematic mechanism and systemic biological applications of the tfLiveDrop reporter in mice. (A) tfLiveDrop mechanism: the mCherry-eGFP-LiveDrop probe specifically localizes to LDs, emitting yellow fluorescence at neutral pH (cytosol/phagophores). Upon lysosomal fusion of autophagomes sequestering LDs, the fluorescence signal of eGFP is quenched, leaving red-only puncta which indirectly reflect the lipophagic flux. (B) Key in vivo findings obtained so far with the tfLiveDrop mice. (i) Basal tissue lipophagy activity . Spatial distribution of lysophagy in adult mice shows high constitutive baseline flux in the liver and intestinal crypts, but quiescence in the brain, heart, lung, and kidney. (ii) Lipophagy in a T2D model . Note the massive accumulation of yellow puncta lagging in red conversion within the liver and kidney, whereas other organs retain normal yellow-to-red transition profiles. (iii) Lipophagy during kidney perinatal development . Longitudinal tracking in AQP1-positive proximal tubules reveals transient cytosolic yellow puncta, de novo LD biosynthesis, at late embryonic (E18.5) and birth (P0) stages, which then converts into red puncta at postnatal week 1 (P7), indicative of an induction of lipophagy, before returning to baseline in adults. Using tfLiveDrop, we mapped basal lipophagic activity across adult mouse organs. Hepatocytes displayed red puncta, reflecting a constitutive lipophagy flux consistent with the liver’s central role in lipid handling. Intestinal crypts, the stem cell niche, also showed clear activity. In striking contrast, kidney, heart, lung, and brain exhibit minimal basal lipophagy under chow diet. We interpret this pattern as indicating that lipophagy acts as a constitutive housekeeper in metabolically active tissues but remains largely quiescent in others, functioning as an “on‑demand” stress response ( Figure 1(B , ⅰ).
